proof:
# Support minorants and common-vertex depth domination

This note proves a comparison theorem for homothetic fibers. It does not
prove the required depth bound for all radius profiles or for general OC.

Let P be a finite nonempty subset of R^n. Let K be a full-dimensional
compact convex body in R^d, d>=1, with centroid zero and volume V. For
p in P let r_p>0 and c_p in R^d, and put K_p=c_p+r_pK. Assume actual
compatibility: for every j in P and every convex representation

    j=sum_p lambda_p p, lambda_p>=0, sum_p lambda_p=1,

one has sum_p lambda_p K_p subset K_j. This holds for actual fibers
of a convex body. Define the finite-fiber measure mu by summing ordinary
d-volume over these lifted fibers. An absolute depth is the infimum
of mu(H) over all closed ambient halfspaces H containing the given
point. The measure has total mass V sum_p r_p^d.

## 1. Finite affine minorants at every sampled base

Suppose real numbers ell_p satisfy

    ell_j <= sum_p lambda_p ell_p                  (1)

for every convex representation of j from P. Then there is b in R^n
such that

    ell_p >= ell_j+b dot(p-j) for every p in P.     (2)

Indeed, the finite linear-inequality alternative applied to the system
b dot(p-j)<=ell_p-ell_j says that infeasibility would give numbers
theta_p>=0 with

    sum_p theta_p(p-j)=0,
    sum_p theta_p(ell_p-ell_j)<0.

Their sum is positive. Dividing by that sum gives a convex representation
of j contradicting(1). This is the ordinary finite Farkas alternative,
with its entire dual certificate displayed; no dimension, interior-point,
or nondegeneracy hypothesis is required. In particular(2) holds at a
boundary base and when P has deficient affine rank.

## 2. Directional comparison at one actual centroid

Fix j in P and a nonzero continuous normal u. Since the centroid of K
is interior, a=-min_(x in K) u dot x is strictly positive. Choose any
minimizing point v in K, so u dot v=-a. Set

    ell_p=u dot c_p-a r_p.

Taking the minimum of u on both sides of the actual Minkowski inclusion
shows exactly(1). Therefore choose b as in(2). It follows that

    u dot(c_p-c_j) >= a(r_p-r_j)+b dot(p-j).        (3)

Any through-(j,c_j) nonvertical cap has the form

    beta dot(p-j)+u dot(x-c_j)>=0.                (4)

Writing x=c_p+r_p X, X in K, its margin is at least

    (beta+b) dot(p-j)+a(r_p-r_j)+r_p u dot X.      (5)

Define the comparison fibers

    L_p=r_j v+r_p(K-v)
        =(r_j-r_p)v+r_p K.                       (6)

Their j-fiber is r_jK, with centroid zero. At the corresponding point
X the margin of the genuine affine cap

    (beta+b) dot(p-j)+u dot x>=0                 (7)

on L_p is exactly(5). The translations from K to the original and
comparison fibers have the same scale r_p, hence the same Jacobian
r_p^d. Pointwise inclusion of the parameter sets where the margins
are nonnegative gives

    mu_original(cap(4)) >= mu_comparison(cap(7)). (8)

This includes equality cases on cut boundaries. For u nonzero those
boundaries have zero d-volume. Purely base-normal caps have identical
whole-fiber masses in the two families and need no minorant.

Equivalently, for X uniform on K let Y=(u dot X+a)/a. Then Y>=0 and
E Y=1, and(8) is the concrete scalar lower bound

    V sum_p r_p^d P{r_p Y>=r_j-w dot(p-j)},
    w=(beta+b)/a.                                (9)

No sum is replaced by an integral in(9). The common normal u is retained
in the single law Y, and there is one adjusted affine base tilt w.

## 3. The comparison is itself a compatible family

Ordinary Brunn--Minkowski applied to the original compatibility gives

    r_k >= sum_p lambda_p r_p                    (10)

for every convex representation of any k in P. Keep the anchor j from
Section2 fixed, and write w0=r_j v. Since0 belongs to K-v, dilations
of K-v are nested. Minkowski addition of nonnegative dilations of a
convex body gives, whenever k=sum_p lambda_p p,

    sum_p lambda_p L_p
      =w0+(sum_p lambda_p r_p)(K-v)
      subset w0+r_k(K-v)=L_k.                    (11)

Here w0=r_j v is the SAME fixed common vertex for all comparison fibers
constructed for the chosen anchor j. Thus this comparison does not
silently violate sampled fiber compatibility.

If P is lattice-convex, its lifted convex hull has exactly these fibers
at every integer base: any point in its j-section is a convex combination
to which(11) applies, and the reverse inclusion is already present.
There are no other integer bases because the projection is conv(P).
The same argument applies to a support of deficient affine rank without
claiming that its hull has ambient interior.

## 4. A single comparison family for all simplex directions and anchors

Now assume K is a simplex. Fix one vertex v0 and put T=K-v0, whose
centroid is g_T=-v0. Define the ONE fixed common-vertex source

    S_star=union_(p in P) {p} x r_p T,
    y_j_star=(j,r_j g_T).                         (12)

For every j one has the absolute-depth domination

    depth_mu_original(j,c_j)
          >= depth_mu_star(y_j_star).            (13)

To prove this, take any original through-point cap with nonzero u. A
linear functional on a simplex has a minimizing vertex, so choose v in
Section2 to be a vertex. There is a linear automorphism A of the centered
simplex K sending v0 to v: take the affine vertex permutation, which
fixes the centroid zero and hence is linear. It preserves K, and
|det A|=1 because it preserves its positive volume. Consequently the
continuous affine map

    x -> A^(-1)(x-r_j v)                          (14)

sends all comparison fibers in(6) to r_p(K-v0)=r_pT, sends the
comparison point zero to-r_j v0, and preserves every fiber volume.
It leaves base coordinates fixed and maps every ambient closed halfspace
to an ambient closed halfspace. In particular(7) becomes a genuine cap
containing y_j_star. Its mass is at least the right side of(13), and
(8) gives the same lower bound for the original cap.

For an original purely base-normal cap, the corresponding cap of S_star
has the identical mass and contains y_j_star. A cap merely containing
the point includes its parallel through-point cap; nonnegativity of
measure completes the proof for all closed containing caps. Taking the
infimum proves(13).

The comparison source(12) is independent of the chosen original normal
and of the anchor j. The maps used to prove the comparison may depend
on both, which is legitimate because each actual cap is bounded below
by the same target depth at the specified comparison point. No claim is
made that one such map sends the entire original body to S_star.

Because S_star itself is a compatible translation arrangement with the
prescribed radii, (13) says that the common-vertex arrangement minimizes
the depth at EACH corresponding own-fiber centroid among all compatible
translation arrangements. The statement concerns these centroids, not
the full maximized depth over every continuous candidate point.

## 5. Scope

The comparison holds for arbitrary finite supports and in every base
dimension n; no integer transformation is used. In particular it
applies to all positive full-dimensional homothetic simplex fibers of
an actual mixed-integer convex body. It can also be used for a polytope
whose affine automorphism group is transitive on its vertices, by the
same minimizing-vertex and volume-preservation argument.

For a general common shape K only the directional comparison(8)-(9)
is asserted; its support minimizer need not be transformable to a fixed
point by an automorphism. Lower-dimensional fibers, nonhomothetic
shapes, and the quantitative OC bound for arbitrary radius profiles
are not supplied by this note. The comparison retains all directions
and does not reduce the positive simplex normal optimization to
coordinate or equal-coefficient normals; the exact triangle example
in `candidate 15438eaf9a458a13` disproves
that further shortcut.

Nor can one assume that some own-fiber centroid reaches OC in the target
family. The archived exact interval example in `candidate 8dd62757ee4f1859`,
under "Every fiber midpoint fails", has consecutive radii(2,6,10,3)
and common-vertex fibers[0,r]. Every own midpoint has absolute depth at
most5, below total mass21 divided by4. This is already a concave,
two-slope radius profile in n=d=1. Thus(13) is not a sufficient all-d
center selection theorem; it is a valid comparison at the specified
points, whose general sufficiency is false.
